Historical Standards & Mathematical Derivation

The Great Wall of China is known in Chinese as the Wanli Changcheng (万里长城, "Ten-Thousand-Li Long Wall"). In Chinese literary culture, "ten thousand" (wan) represents an infinite, immense number. In the Qin and Han dynasties (when the wall was first consolidated), 10,000 Han li equaled approx. 4,158 kilometers (2,584 miles), remarkably close to the primary rampart's length.

Primary Source References:
Hanshu (Book of Han: Treatise on Metrology); Qing Huidian (Collected Statutes of the Qing Dynasty); Needham, Science and Civilisation in China.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long is a Chinese li in kilometers and miles?
In the modern market system (shi li), 1 li equals exactly 500 meters (0.5 km or 0.3107 miles). In imperial times, it varied: Han dynasty li was 415.8 meters, Tang was 531 meters, and Qing was 576 meters.
Why is the Great Wall called 10,000 Li?
Because the number 10,000 (wan, 万) in Chinese is symbolic of vast, epic scale. At 415.8 meters per Han dynasty li, 10,000 li equaled 4,158 km, closely approximating the wall's historical expanse.
